body.en: Every quadratic \( ax^2+bx+c=0 \) with real coefficients has solutions — as long as we're willing to accept square roots of negative numbers. Complex numbers make that promise precise: they extend \( \mathbb{R} \) just enough that every polynomial equation gets a solution, using one new symbol, \( i \), and the ordinary rules of algebra everywhere else.

label.en: ● Definition 1.1 — The imaginary unit and complex numbers

body.en: The imaginary unit \( i \) satisfies \( i^2=-1 \). A complex number is any expression \( z=a+bi \) with \( a,b\in\mathbb{R} \): \( a \) is the real part, written \( \operatorname{Re}(z) \), and \( b \) is the imaginary part, written \( \operatorname{Im}(z) \). When \( b=0 \), \( z \) is an ordinary real number; when \( a=0 \) and \( b\neq0 \), \( z \) is called purely imaginary.
Complex numbers add and multiply exactly like binomials in \( a+bx \) form — the only extra rule is \( i^2=-1 \), which you use to simplify after multiplying out.

For \( z_1=a+bi \) and \( z_2=c+di \):

\[ z_1+z_2=(a+c)+(b+d)i \]

\[ z_1 z_2=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i \]

The multiplication rule is just FOIL followed by \( i^2\to -1 \): \( (a+bi)(c+di)=ac+adi+bci+bdi^2=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i \).

The complex conjugate of \( z=a+bi \) is \( \bar z=a-bi \) — same real part, opposite sign on the imaginary part. The modulus (or absolute value) of \( z \) is \[ |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}, \] the distance from \( z \) to the origin when \( z \) is plotted as the point \( (a,b) \) in the complex plane.
For every complex number \( z=a+bi \), \[ z\bar z=|z|^2. \] In particular \( z\bar z \) is always a nonnegative real number.

Write \( z=a+bi \), so \( \bar z=a-bi \). Multiplying directly (Definition 1.2, with \( c=a,\,d=-b \)):

\[ z\bar z=(a+bi)(a-bi)=\big[a\cdot a-b\cdot(-b)\big]+\big[a\cdot(-b)+b\cdot a\big]i=(a^2+b^2)+0i=a^2+b^2. \]

Since \( |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), squaring both sides gives \( |z|^2=a^2+b^2 \), which is exactly what the product \( z\bar z \) equals. Hence \( z\bar z=|z|^2 \), and this is nonnegative since it's a sum of two squares. \( \blacksquare \)
Theorem 1.1 is exactly what makes complex division possible: to divide by \( z_2 \), multiply top and bottom by \( \bar z_2 \) so the denominator becomes the real number \( |z_2|^2 \).

Simplify \( \dfrac{5+i}{2-3i} \).

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, \( 2+3i \):

\[ \frac{5+i}{2-3i}\cdot\frac{2+3i}{2+3i}=\frac{(5+i)(2+3i)}{(2-3i)(2+3i)}. \]

Numerator: \( (5)(2)-(1)(3)+\big[(5)(3)+(1)(2)\big]i=10-3+17i=7+17i \). Denominator, by Theorem 1.1: \( |2-3i|^2=2^2+3^2=13 \). So

\[ \frac{5+i}{2-3i}=\frac{7+17i}{13}=\frac{7}{13}+\frac{17}{13}i. \]
